title: Infrastructure as code, Azure Resource Manager and ARM templates
learningObjective: Describe infrastructure as code, Azure Resource Manager, and the benefits of ARM templates and Bicep.
foundation: Infrastructure as code (IaC): describe your infrastructure in files (code) instead of clicking through the portal. Deploy the same file again and you get the same environment every time.

Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is the deployment and management service for Azure. Every request (from the portal, CLI, PowerShell, SDKs or templates) goes through it, which applies authentication, RBAC, Policy and locks.
ARM templates are JSON files that describe the resources you want. Bicep is a simpler language that compiles to ARM templates. Both are declarative: you say what you want, not how to build it.
engineer: Resource Manager benefits: manage infrastructure through declarative templates; deploy, manage and monitor resources as a group; redeploy consistently; define dependencies so resources deploy in the right order; apply access control (RBAC) and tags; see costs grouped by tag.

ARM template benefits: declarative syntax; repeatable results (idempotent: deploy many times, same result); orchestration (Resource Manager orders dependent resources and deploys in parallel when possible); modular files (linked and nested templates); extensibility (deployment scripts); built-in validation before deployment; tracked deployments (history in the portal); what-if previews; export templates from existing resources.
Deployment modes: Incremental (default: add or update resources in the template, leave others alone) and Complete (also delete resources in the resource group that aren't in the template).

Bicep: concise syntax, type safety and modules; same capabilities as JSON ARM templates; deployed with the same commands (az deployment group create). Other IaC tools such as Terraform also work with Azure through Resource Manager.
IaC practice: store templates in source control, review changes in pull requests, deploy with pipelines (GitHub Actions, Azure Pipelines), and parameterise per environment (dev, test, prod).

example.title: Three identical environments
body: A team defines its app's VNet, App Service and SQL database in one Bicep file with parameters for size and name. A pipeline deploys it to dev, test and prod.
When a setting changes, they edit the file and redeploy: only the difference is applied. A what-if run before production shows exactly what will change.

prerequisites: An Azure subscription (a free account works)
permissions: Reader to explore; Contributor to create resources
portal: Resource group > Deployments: history and templates.
Create a resource > Template deployment (deploy using custom templates).
configuration.cli:
az deployment group what-if -g rg-app --template-file main.bicep --parameters env=test
az deployment group create -g rg-app --template-file main.bicep --parameters env=test

troubleshooting.symptom: A resource disappeared after a template deployment.
troubleshooting.cause: Complete mode removed resources not in the template.
troubleshooting.fix: Use incremental mode, or add the resource to the template; run what-if first.

troubleshooting.symptom: Deployment fails because the VM is created before its NIC.
troubleshooting.fix: Reference the NIC (Bicep infers dependencies) or add dependsOn.

comparisons.difference: Templates describe the end state; scripts list commands to run in order.
Same engine; Bicep is shorter and easier to read and compiles to JSON.

misconceptions.myth: Templates are only for creating resources once.
misconceptions.reality: Redeploying updates resources to match the file.

misconceptions.myth: ARM is only used by templates.
misconceptions.reality: Every Azure management request goes through Resource Manager.

misconceptions.myth: Bicep needs a separate deployment service.

architectureDecisions: Keep infrastructure in source control as Bicep.
Use incremental mode and what-if by default.
Deploy with pipelines, not by hand.
